The Profit Quality Test
CFO ÷ NI over 3 years: above 0.8 is good, below 0.5 needs a close look.
Receivables growth against sales: sales up 30% and receivables up 90% = low-quality profit.
Inventory growth against sales: building inventory can precede a write-down or falling demand.
Maintenance CAPEX against depreciation: with inflation, historical depreciation is far below replacement cost; part of the profit must be set aside for replacement.

Estimating Sustainable Profit
Build It from the Bottom Up
1. Sales volume: the average of the last 12 months, adjusted for new capacity or a known constraint.
2. Selling price: the latest monthly price, not last year’s average. Exports: dollar price × the exchange rate available to the company.
3. Cost of sales: the materials-to-sales ratio from the notes; formula-priced feedstock at the current formula.
4. General and administrative expenses: last year × (1 + expected inflation).
5. Finance costs and tax: at current debt and rates.
6. Divide by the share count after the latest registered or confirmed capital increase.

Earnings Yield Against Akhza
E/P in a Country with High-Yield Akhza
E/P = sustainable EPS ÷ price.
When Akhza has a high nominal yield, a low P/E alone doesn’t mean cheap.
The expected return must exceed the Akhza yield + a risk premium (say 5 to 10 percentage points).
Example: E/P 20%, payout 60%, growth 25% → 20 × 0.6 + 25 = 37% against a hypothetical 30% Akhza → a thin margin of safety.

Payback and Profit Quality
The Payback Period
How many years until the sum of EPS (with growth) reaches today’s price?
Price 100, first-year EPS 20, growth 25% → 20, 25, 31.25, 39.06 → 76.25 after 3 years and 115.3 after 4 years → about 3.6 years.
FIS rule of thumb: prefer a payback under about 4 to 5 years with sustainable profit and conservative growth. The threshold is a judgement call; adjust it to the day’s risk-free rate.
Profit Quality and Replacement Value
The same E/P is worth more for a company with high CFO/NI, little debt and pricing power. For low-quality profit use a lower target P/E.
For asset-heavy companies (cement, mining, holdings), replacement value or NAV is a useful analytical floor.
A price below replacement value is no reason to buy on its own if the factory doesn’t make a profit.
